17   POOLER, Circuit Judge:

18         Courts face unique difficulties when conflicting constitutional rights are at

19   stake. The right to protest is a fundamental right central to the First Amendment.

20   The right to be free from harassment and threats from protestors is an equally

21   fundamental right. Properly protecting both sets of rights presents some of the

22   most challenging work courts are called upon to do.

23         Helpfully, decisions of the legislature sometimes guide us in conducting

24   this delicate balancing task. With respect to protests outside reproductive health

25   clinics, Congress, the State of New York, and New York City have enacted laws

26   that delineate the line between appropriate protest activities and those that
                                              4
  1   infringe improperly on the right of those attempting to access the clinic. This case

 2   requires us to define the scope of the federal Freedom of Access to Clinic

 3   Entrances (“FACE”) Act and its state and local counterparts.

 4           Every Saturday morning in Queens, New York, anti-abortion groups

 5   have protested outside Choices Medical Center, a reproductive health care

 6   facility offering a myriad of reproductive health services, including abortions.

 7   The protestors contend that their efforts walk up to, but do not cross, the legal

 8   boundary. These protestors employ tactics like “do[ing] the slow walk in front of

 9   the clients so [other protestors] can talk to [those patients],” because it “gives

10   [them] a little more time to plead for the baby’s life,” App’x at 1860; “tag

11   teaming” patients so that, even after a patient has asked the protestor to leave her

12   alone, another protestor will approach the patient, App’x at 1750; or using signs

13   as a “barrier” by the clinic entrance on a city sidewalk, App’x at 1881.

14         After a yearlong investigation into the protestor activity outside Choices,

15   the New York Office of the Attorney General (“OAG”) brought suit and sought a

16   preliminary injunction against certain protestors, including Defendants Kenneth

17   Griepp, Ronald George, Patricia Musco, Ranville Thomas, Osayinwense

18   Okuonghae, Anne Kaminsky, Brian George, Sharon Richards, Deborah Ryan,
                                               5
  1   Prisca Joseph, Angela Braxton, Jasmine LaLande, and Scott Fitchett, Jr.

 2   (collectively “Defendants”) relating to their protest activities in violation of the

 3   federal Freedom of Access to Clinic Entrances Act (“FACE”), 18 U.S.C.

 4   § 248(a)(1), (c)(3)(A); the New York Clinic Access Act (“NYSCAA”), N.Y. Penal

 5   Law § 240.70(1)(a)-(b); and the New York City Clinic Access Act (“the City Act”),

 6   N.Y.C. Admin. Code §§ 10-1003(a)(1)-(4), 10-1004.

 7         In its denial of the preliminary injunction, which the OAG appeals before

 8   us today, the district court concluded that Defendants’ conduct was too minor to

 9   constitute violations of FACE and its state and local analogs. It characterized the

10   challenged protestor activity as merely “incidental contact,” causing only

11   “slight[]” deviations or delays, or otherwise being too negligible to interfere with

12   patients’ rights. New York by Underwood v. Griepp, No. 17-CV-3706, 2018 WL

13   3518527, at *33, *44 (E.D.N.Y. July 20, 2018).

14         We cannot completely agree with the district court’s conclusions. FACE is

15   by its own terms broad. Writing in restrictions to narrow its reach, in

16   contravention of its text and purpose, would effectively eviscerate the statute.

17   Because we determine that the district court made certain improper evidentiary

18   and credibility rulings, relied on clearly erroneous factual findings in assessing
                                               6
  1   the OAG’s physical obstruction claims, erred in its interpretation of the FACE

 2   statute and its state and local analogs, and abused its discretion in finding no

 3   irreparable harm, we vacate and remand in part. 2 We affirm as to the remainder.

 4         Defendants also cross-appeal from the same order denying the preliminary

 5   injunction. Defendants challenge the following conclusions of the district court:

 6   (1) Defendant Brian George violated FACE, NYSCAA, and the City Act by

 7   physically obstructing patients; (2) the statutes do not violate the First

 8   Amendment; and (3) the OAG has parens patriae standing to sue under the City

 9   Act. We affirm the district court’s conclusions on these issues.

10                                    BACKGROUND

11   I.    Choices Medical Center

12         Choices Medical Center (“Choices”) is an ambulatory outpatient medical

13   center that provides extensive reproductive health services in Jamaica, Queens,

     brackets, and quotation marks omitted). In using the term “abuse of discretion”
     in this opinion, we therefore mean no slight to the able district court in this case.

 2   colposcopy, and obstetrics and gynecological services, among others. The main

 3   entrance is located on 147th Place between Jamaica and Archer Avenues, but

 4   there is also an employee entrance on 148th Street between Jamaica and Archer

 5   Avenues and a patient exit on Jamaica Avenue between 147th Place and 148th

 6   Street. Most patients arrive by foot and enter through the main entrance. Other

 7   patients arrive by cars, which drop them off on 147th Place next to the main

 8   entrance.

 9         Every Saturday morning since the clinic first opened in 2012, people have

10   protested outside the main entrance. While some protestors are independent

11   individuals, most are affiliated with organized groups such as Church at the

12   Rock or Grace Baptist Church. 3 Protestors from Church at the Rock are typically

13   assigned roles including preaching, sidewalk counseling, handing out literature,

14   or holding large signs.

 2   volunteer “escorts” greet and walk patients down the sidewalk to the main

 3   entrance when protestors are present. These escorts arrive on Saturday mornings

 4   and are present from the clinic’s opening at 7:00 am until the protestors’

10   block their visibility. On an average Saturday morning, there are two to three

11   dozen protestors and escorts.

12   II.   The Attorney General’s Investigation

13         In June 2016, the OAG began a year-long investigation into the protest

14   activity outside Choices. As part of its investigation, it installed a high-mounted

15   surveillance camera to capture the 147th Place entrance, and it also used

16   undercover investigators with hidden cameras to pose as patients and their




                                               9
  1   companions. Two escort leaders, 4 Pearl Brady and Theresa White, aided the

 2   investigation by wearing hidden cameras on a few occasions.

 3   III.   Procedural History

 4          A. Preliminary Injunction Hearing

 5          On June 20, 2017, the OAG, on behalf of the State of New York as parens

 6   patriae, sued thirteen protestors for purported violations of FACE, 18 U.S.C.

 7   § 248(a)(1), (c)(3)(A); the NYSCAA, N.Y. Penal Law § 240.70(1)(a)-(b); and the

 8   City Act, N.Y.C. Admin. Code §§ 10-1003(a)(1)-(4), 10-1004. In broad strokes, the

 9   OAG alleged that Defendants violated these laws by crowding patients and

10   escorts with their bodies and signs, leaning into cars to provide literature or

11   counseling, making threatening statements, and attempting to engage patients

12   and escorts despite clear rebuffs. The OAG also filed a motion for a preliminary

13   injunction the same day it filed its complaint. Shortly thereafter, Defendants filed

14   motions to dismiss and opposed the motion for a preliminary injunction.




     4 The escort program at Choices included volunteer escorts, who receive no
     compensation, and escort leaders, who receive reimbursement from Choices for

 5   introduced three types of evidence: documentary evidence, video and

 7   ten defendants’ witnesses.

 8         The documentary evidence consisted of two types of records kept by the

 9   clinic: Clinic Escort Recaps (“Recaps”) and Protestor Experience Questionnaires

10   (“PEQs”). The Recaps provide an overview of the day’s events and any

11   noteworthy incidents. Various escorts or escort leaders draft the Recaps, but the

12   author of a given Recap is only sometimes apparent from the face of the

13   document. The PEQs are filled out by patients after entering the clinic and are

14   meant to collect information from the patients’ perspectives as to whether they

15   encountered protestors, and if so, whether the protestors touched them or tried

16   to prevent them from accessing the clinic’s entrance. The PEQs included both

17   yes/no questions and open-ended ones.

 9         B. The District Court’s Decision

10         On July 20, 2018, the district court denied the OAG’s motion for a

11   preliminary injunction.

18   not credible because advice she gave to her fellow escorts on how to testify

                                              13

 6         Based on the remaining credible evidence, the district court held that the

11   As a summary of its overarching conclusions, the district court said that the

14         The sole challenged act that was ultimately held to be a violation was

15   defendant B. George’s “slow walk,” a tactic B. George used to delay patients and

16   their companions to provide more time for anti-abortion counseling. Griepp, 2018

13         In the same July 20, 2018 order, the district court rejected the claims

18         Both parties timely appealed.
                                               15
  1                                      DISCUSSION

 2         The issues presented to us by the appeal are: (1) whether the district court

 3   erred in finding not reliable all the OAG’s documentary evidence and the bulk of

 4   its testimonial evidence; (2) whether the OAG demonstrated a likelihood of

 5   success on the merits of its FACE, NYSCAA, and City Act claims; and (3)

 6   whether the OAG demonstrated irreparable harm.

 7         The issues presented by the cross-appeal are: (1) whether FACE, NYSCAA,

 8   and the City Act are facially constitutional; (2) whether the OAG has parens

 9   patriae standing to sue under the City Act; and (3) whether defendant B. George

10   impermissibly engaged in physical obstruction by using a slow walk to delay

11   patients accessing the facility.

12   I.    Evidentiary Rulings

13         We review a lower court’s credibility determinations for clear error. United

14   States v. Monzon, 359 F.3d 110, 119 (2d Cir. 2004). Although this standard is

15   deferential, we have reversed credibility determinations in some instances, such

16   as when the credibility assessment cannot be reconciled with other evidence,

17   when the district court incorrectly assessed the probative value of pieces of

18   evidence, when it relied on speculation, or when the determinations were
                                             16
  1   “founded on factual inferences that the evidence did not permit.” Doe v. Menefee,

 2   391 F.3d 147, 164 (2d Cir. 2004).

 3         The OAG challenges the district court’s failure to give any weight to the

 4   Recaps and PEQs along with its adverse credibility determinations regarding

 5   five of its witnesses. We address each in turn.

 6         A. Documentary Evidence

 7         The district court did not assign any weight to the documentary

 8   evidence—the Recaps and the PEQs—for three reasons: (1) the evidence was

 9   hearsay, and because the parties had conducted discovery and presented live

10   testimony, there was no need to consider hearsay; (2) the Recaps, according to

11   the district court, tended to exaggerate the impropriety of protestor conduct; and

12   (3) because escort program director Greenberg destroyed a number of the PEQs

13   without having a system guiding her process, the PEQs’ representative value

14   was not ascertainable. We conclude that none of these is a valid basis upon

15   which to categorically reject the evidence. Therefore, failing to consider the

16   Recaps and PEQs was clear error.

17         In reaching this conclusion, we emphasize that the district court’s

18   categorical exclusion of this admissible evidence is the error. The dissent takes
                                              17
  1   issue with what it perceives to be an imposition of our credibility determination

 2   in the place of the district court’s, interpreting our decision as requiring the

 3   district court to accept the Recaps and PEQs as entirely credible. 6 We do no such

 4   thing. We instead rely on applicable precedent instructing us that categorical

 5   exclusion of this evidence was error.

 6                1. Hearsay

 7         As the district court correctly noted, hearsay evidence is admissible in a

 8   preliminary injunction hearing. Mullins v. City of New York, 626 F.3d 47, 52 (2d

 9   Cir. 2010). But while the district court properly admitted the Recaps and PEQs, it

10   erred in concluding that the Recaps and PEQs categorically “deserve[d] no

11   weight” because, having completed discovery and taken live testimony from

12   seventeen witnesses, “the urgency usually supporting the use of hearsay

13   testimony in this setting” was missing. Griepp, 2018 WL 3518527, at *5.

14          In Mullins, we explained that rejecting hearsay evidence at the preliminary

15   injunction stage “would be at odds with the summary nature of the remedy and




     6As the partial dissent notes, there are many points on which the entire panel
     agrees. I refer to this partial dissent and partial concurrence as “the dissent” for
     ease of reading.
                                                18
  1   would undermine the ability of courts to provide timely provisional relief.” 626

 2   F.3d at 52. Excluding documents exclusively because they are hearsay in a

 3   preliminary injunction hearing is thus at odds with our precedent. This is true

 4   regardless of whether testimony has been taken or discovery completed. Indeed,

 5   in Mullins itself, discovery had concluded and depositions had been taken. Id. at

 6   50-51. The district court here was permitted, under Mullins, to admit hearsay

 7   despite the somewhat unusual procedural posture at hand.

 8         Citing to Mullins, see Griepp, 2018 WL 3518527, at *5, the district court

 9   correctly admitted the Recaps and PEQs, but it erred in categorically giving them

10   no weight. We recognize that a trier of fact has considerable discretion in

11   weighing the evidence before it. But the district court’s reason for ignoring the

12   documentary evidence here—that this evidence was both unnecessary and

13   inherently unreliable—functionally contravenes the principle we articulated in

14   Mullins, that “[t]he admissibility of hearsay . . . goes to weight, not preclusion, at

15   the preliminary injunction stage.” 626 F.3d at 52. Categorically giving no weight

16   to the Recaps and PEQs on this basis was therefore erroneous. See Bradford Tr. Co.

17   of Bos. v. Merrill Lynch, Pierce, Fenner & Smith, Inc., 805 F.2d 49, 55 (2d Cir. 1986)

18   (explaining that the district court’s decision to ignore evidence properly admitted
                                                19
  1   under the public records exception because it was hearsay “is inconsistent with

 2   the notion of having exceptions to the hearsay rule[;] [c]onsequently, it was error

 3   for the trial court after admitting the FBI reports to accord them no weight”). 7

 4         Thus, the district court’s categorical exclusion of the documentary

 5   evidence cannot be supported by the hearsay nature of the evidence. We now

 6   turn to the district court’s additional justifications.

 7                2. Escort Recaps

 8         Notwithstanding the deference we give to a district court’s credibility

 9   determinations, we conclude that the district court clearly erred in giving no

10   weight to the Recaps as a category. The district court chose not to give weight to

11   these documents because “they tend to exaggerate the impropriety of protestor

12   conduct and generally fail to provide . . . context.” Griepp, 2018 WL 3518527, at *5.

13   Yet the court only referenced one Recap with an apparent inconsistency to

14   support this sweeping characterization.



     7The dissent argues that the facts and circumstances of a given case should
     dictate a district court’s approach to assigning weight to hearsay evidence. We
     do not disagree with that principle. But, as we make clear below, it was the
     district court’s blanket approach to discrediting the Recaps and PEQs—largely
     because they constituted hearsay—that did not account for the facts and
     circumstances of the present case.
                                               20
  1         Even if the district court had grounds to assign little evidentiary weight to

 2   that particular Recap on credibility grounds, it was inappropriate to dismiss

 3   every Recap based on exaggeration in one. Each Recap described different

 4   incidents from different shifts, based on the recollections of distinct groups of

 5   volunteer escorts. Therefore, even if a few authors exaggerated, the exaggeration

 6   in one or two Recaps may not necessarily appear in others. The district court’s

 7   categorical exclusion of all Recaps based on one of them assumes that all these

 8   documents share the identified infirmities—but this is a factual inference the

 9   evidence does not permit.

10         Nor is there valid reason to believe that all escorts tend to exaggerate. The

11   district court suggested that the escorts were biased because of their views.

12   Defendants no less than escorts have firm convictions about abortion—but

13   Defendants were nevertheless considered credible. This alone, then, cannot

14   support a finding of bias. Without more to corroborate such a finding as to all

15   escorts who contributed to the Recaps, the categorical exclusion of these

16   documents lacks the necessary support.

17         Defendants point to an additional Recap to suggest the Recaps are

18   unreliable. The Recap notes that defendant Musco “used both hands to push
                                              21
  1   escorts who were blocking her access to a patient near the entrance.” App’x at

 2   2318. Defendants argue that, during the hearing, escort Garnick admitted the

 3   Recap was inaccurate after viewing a video clip. That is not so. Garnick testified

 4   that the shoving incident “isn’t [in the clip]. However, prior to that was what I

 5   believe I testified to.” App’x at 1426. We fail to see how this is an inconsistency.

 6         Even if there were an additional incorrect Recap, two unreliable

 7   documents still would not justify categorical exclusion. Given the variation in

 8   authorship, there is simply no logical basis to suggest all Recaps are similarly

 9   defective. As a sister circuit has noted, because of the substantial risk that they

10   are arbitrary and overbroad, such blanket evidentiary rulings are strongly

11   disfavored. See Cerabio LLC v. Wright Med. Tech., Inc., 410 F.3d 981, 994 (7th Cir.

12   2005). Rather, the district court should have considered the evidence

13   individually. Id. By instead categorically rejecting all Recaps based on its

14   concerns about one of those documents, the district court abused its discretion.

15                3. Protestor Experience Questionnaires

16         Giving no weight to the PEQs because of concerns over the PEQs’

17   representative value was also clear error. The district court concluded that the

18   “representative value” of the PEQs was “impossible to ascertain” because “only
                                              22
  1   a sample” was presented to the court and because escort program director

 2   Greenberg destroyed many of them. Griepp, 2018 WL 3518527, at *6. 8 The PEQs’

12   many of the exhibits discussed above, we have affirmed the district court’s

16                2. Threats of force

17         FACE proscribes making a “threat of force,” which our Circuit has

18   interpreted to mean only true threats not protected under the First Amendment.
                                               60
  1   Operation Rescue, 273 F.3d at 194. When reviewing a district court’s determination

 2   on the issue of whether particular speech was a true threat, we conduct an

 3   independent examination of the record as a whole. Id. at 196.

 4         To determine whether speech is a true threat, we ask whether an ordinary,

 5   reasonable recipient familiar with the context of the communication would

 6   interpret the speech as a threat of injury. United States v. Turner, 720 F.3d 411, 420

 7   & n.4 (2d Cir. 2013). Our inquiry is informed by whether the threat is, on its face

 8   and under the circumstances, so “unequivocal, unconditional, immediate and

 9   specific as to the person threatened as to convey a gravity of purpose and

10   imminent prospect of execution.” Operation Rescue, 273 F.3d at 196. However, we

11   have still found threats “that were both conditional and inexplicit.” Turner, 720

12   F.3d at 424. Nor is there any requirement that the statements on their face show

13   that the defendant personally intended to take violent action, id., but the

14   recipient must be afraid of the threat’s execution by the speaker or their co-

15   conspirators, Operation Rescue, 273 F.3d at 196.

16         Context is also critical. For instance, in United States v. Dillard, the reference

17   of a murdered abortion provider in a letter gave it “an additional threatening

18   undertone.” 795 F.3d 1191, 1201 (10th Cir. 2015). In Dillard, the defendant sent a
                                               61

 4   persuade Dr. Means to change her plans, writing, “[i]f Tiller could speak from

 5   hell, he would tell you what a soulless existence you are purposefully

11   FACE, alleging that the defendant’s letter constituted a threat of force against Dr.

12   Means. Id. at 1197-98. The district court in Dillard granted summary judgment

14   likely, or unconditional and because the letter said nothing about what the

 8                3. Force

 9         Neither FACE nor NYSCAA define “force,” but this Circuit has held in the

10   context of a different federal statute that “force” broadly means “power,

11   violence, or pressure directed against a person or thing.” Dickson v. Ashcroft, 346

12   F.3d 44, 50 (2d Cir. 2003) (citation omitted). It is not limited to violent or

13   assaultive force. Id. Because this definition accords with the common meaning of

14   the term, we adopt this definition of “force” for FACE purposes.

15         The OAG argues that Exhibit 21, the only piece of evidence the district

16   court considered, shows that force was used by the protestors. The district court

17   stated, however, that while the video shows a collision between defendant

18   LaLande and an escort, it is not clear who initiated contact. Griepp, 2018 WL
                                                77
  1   3518527, at *33. The district court said this was “quintessential incidental contact,

 2   because neither LaLande nor the escorts appear to be trying to create a collision.

 3   Rather, it appears that LaLande was trying to hand the patient a pamphlet while

 4   the escorts tried to block her access to the patient.” Id. (citation omitted). As such,

 5   the conduct was not undertaken with the intent to injure, intimidate, or interfere.

 6   Id. We agree with the district court’s ultimate conclusion for different reasons.

 7         We disagree with the notion that incidental contact cannot rise to a FACE

 8   force violation. As the legislative history of FACE makes clear, the requirement

 9   that defendants “intentionally injure, intimidate, or interfere” means only that

10   the defendant “intends to perform the act and is aware of the natural and

11   probable consequences.” S. Rep. No. 103-117, at 24 n.39. Under this definition of

12   intent, incidental contact is not excluded from the statute’s scope. For example, a

13   protestor who reaches out to hand a patient a pamphlet and collides with the

14   patient as a result will have intentionally interfered with, intimidated, or injured

15   the patient, so long as: (1) the protestor intended to reach out; (2) the contact was

16   the natural and probable result of reaching out; and (3) the protestor was aware

17   that the contact was the natural and probable consequence of reaching out. That

18   the interference, intimidation, or injury was a byproduct, rather than the goal, of
                                               78
  1   reaching out is thus not dispositive. Rather, intent turns upon whether a result

 2   was likely—that is, the natural and probable consequence—of a defendant’s

 3   action and whether the defendant was aware of this.

 4         This understanding of FACE’s intent requirement accords with that of

 5   other Circuits as well. For instance, in Dillard, the Tenth Circuit addressed the

 6   defendant’s argument that there was no evidence that she subjectively intended

 7   to injure, intimidate, or interfere with the provision of abortion services when she

 9   F.3d at 1202-03. The defendant had repeatedly made statements that she did not

10   approve of violence or intend to threaten Dr. Means or others. Id. at 1202-03.

11   Though the Tenth Circuit acknowledged that there is a subjective intent

12   requirement, it held that the relevant showing may be satisfied from the evidence

13   of the act itself because “normally the actor is presumed to have intended the

14   natural consequences of his deeds.” Id. at 1202 (quoting Washington v. Davis, 426

15   U.S. 229, 253 (1976) (Stevens, J., concurring)). Because “the government ha[d]

16   presented evidence from which a jury could reasonably find that [the d]efendant

17   intentionally mailed Dr. Means a letter which contains a threat of violence,” there

  1   was evidence in Dillard “that [the defendant] subjectively intended the natural

11   otherwise subjects such other person to physical contact, or attempts or threatens

12   to do the same; . . . follows a person in or about a public place or places; or . . .

13   engages in a course of conduct or repeatedly commits acts which alarm or

14   seriously annoy such other person and which serve no legitimate purpose,” N.Y.

15   Penal Law § 240.26. In analyzing the terms “intent to harass, annoy or alarm

16   another” and “legitimate purpose,” as relevant here, we are guided by state court

17   precedent.

  1         We agree with the district court that defendant B. George’s slow walk was

13   to portions of the challenged conduct in its preliminary injunction analysis and

15   the merits, we hold that FACE and its analogs proscribe delaying patients

   A. Physical Obstruction

      As relevant to physical obstruction, a person violates FACE and the State

Act when, “by physical obstruction,” he or she “intentionally injures, intimidates,

or interferes with” another person (or attempts to do so) “because that person is

or has been . . . obtaining or providing reproductive health services.” 18 U.S.C.

§ 248(a)(1) (emphasis added); see also N.Y. Penal Law § 240.70(3)(c). Both statutes

define “physical obstruction” as “rendering impassable ingress to or egress from a

facility that provides reproductive health services . . . , or rendering passage to or

from such a facility . . . unreasonably difficult or hazardous.” 18 U.S.C. § 248(e)(4)

(emphases added); see also N.Y. Penal Law § 240.70(3)(d).

“illegal interference with clinic access,” but not to stifle “legitimate protest

activities,” Operation Rescue, 273 F.3d at 195, the majority suggests that FACE (and

the almost identically worded State Act) are violated by, inter alia, “delaying

patients even for a brief amount of time” to offer a pamphlet, standing on a

sidewalk holding a sign in an area where no clinic visitors are to be found, and by

17   POOLER, Circuit Judge:

18         Courts face unique difficulties when conflicting constitutional rights are at

19   stake. The right to protest is a fundamental right central to the First Amendment.

20   The right to be free from harassment and threats from protestors is an equally

21   fundamental right. Properly protecting both sets of rights presents some of the

22   most challenging work courts are called upon to do.

23         Helpfully, decisions of the legislature sometimes guide us in conducting

24   this delicate balancing task. With respect to protests outside reproductive health

25   clinics, Congress, the State of New York, and New York City have enacted laws

26   that delineate the line between appropriate protest activities and those that
                                              4
  1   infringe improperly on the right of those attempting to access the clinic. This case

 2   requires us to define the scope of the federal Freedom of Access to Clinic

 3   Entrances (“FACE”) Act and its state and local counterparts.

 4           Every Saturday morning in Queens, New York, anti-abortion groups

 5   have protested outside Choices Medical Center, a reproductive health care

 6   facility offering a myriad of reproductive health services, including abortions.

 7   The protestors contend that their efforts walk up to, but do not cross, the legal

 8   boundary. These protestors employ tactics like “do[ing] the slow walk in front of

 9   the clients so [other protestors] can talk to [those patients],” because it “gives

10   [them] a little more time to plead for the baby’s life,” App’x at 1860; “tag

11   teaming” patients so that, even after a patient has asked the protestor to leave her

12   alone, another protestor will approach the patient, App’x at 1750; or using signs

13   as a “barrier” by the clinic entrance on a city sidewalk, App’x at 1881.

 2         The issues presented to us by the appeal are: (1) whether the district court

 3   erred in finding not reliable all the OAG’s documentary evidence and the bulk of

 4   its testimonial evidence; (2) whether the OAG demonstrated a likelihood of

 5   success on the merits of its FACE, NYSCAA, and City Act claims; and (3)

 6   whether the OAG demonstrated irreparable harm.

 7         The issues presented by the cross-appeal are: (1) whether FACE, NYSCAA,

 8   and the City Act are facially constitutional; (2) whether the OAG has parens

 9   patriae standing to sue under the City Act; and (3) whether defendant B. George

10   impermissibly engaged in physical obstruction by using a slow walk to delay

11   patients accessing the facility.

12   I.    Evidentiary Rulings

13         We review a lower court’s credibility determinations for clear error. United

14   States v. Monzon,
359 F.3d 110, 119
 (2d Cir. 2004). Although this standard is

15   deferential, we have reversed credibility determinations in some instances, such

16   as when the credibility assessment cannot be reconciled with other evidence,

17   when the district court incorrectly assessed the probative value of pieces of

18   evidence, when it relied on speculation, or when the determinations were

 3         The OAG challenges the district court’s failure to give any weight to the

 4   Recaps and PEQs along with its adverse credibility determinations regarding

 5   five of its witnesses. We address each in turn.

 6         A. Documentary Evidence

 7         The district court did not assign any weight to the documentary

 8   evidence—the Recaps and the PEQs—for three reasons: (1) the evidence was

 9   hearsay, and because the parties had conducted discovery and presented live

10   testimony, there was no need to consider hearsay; (2) the Recaps, according to

11   the district court, tended to exaggerate the impropriety of protestor conduct; and

12   (3) because escort program director Greenberg destroyed a number of the PEQs

13   without having a system guiding her process, the PEQs’ representative value

14   was not ascertainable. We conclude that none of these is a valid basis upon

15   which to categorically reject the evidence. Therefore, failing to consider the

16   Recaps and PEQs was clear error.

17         In reaching this conclusion, we emphasize that the district court’s

18   categorical exclusion of this admissible evidence is the error. The dissent takes

 7         We disagree with the notion that incidental contact cannot rise to a FACE

 8   force violation. As the legislative history of FACE makes clear, the requirement

 9   that defendants “intentionally injure, intimidate, or interfere” means only that

10   the defendant “intends to perform the act and is aware of the natural and

11   probable consequences.” S. Rep. No. 103-117, at 24 n.39. Under this definition of

12   intent, incidental contact is not excluded from the statute’s scope. For example, a

13   protestor who reaches out to hand a patient a pamphlet and collides with the

14   patient as a result will have intentionally interfered with, intimidated, or injured

15   the patient, so long as: (1) the protestor intended to reach out; (2) the contact was

16   the natural and probable result of reaching out; and (3) the protestor was aware

17   that the contact was the natural and probable consequence of reaching out. That

18   the interference, intimidation, or injury was a byproduct, rather than the goal, of
                                               78
  1   reaching out is thus not dispositive. Rather, intent turns upon whether a result

 2   was likely—that is, the natural and probable consequence—of a defendant’s

      We warned in Operation Rescue that courts must not “characterize[]

legitimate protest activities as illegal interference with clinic access.”
273 F.3d at 195
. We noted that special care must be taken in this context, lest the erroneous

application of statutes by courts “impinge legitimate First Amendment activity.”
Id.
 Some issues invariably inspire great passion. But dearly held beliefs are no

excuse for torturing statutory language, abandoning precedent, and jettisoning

carefully reasoned and amply supported district court findings, particularly when

First Amendment freedoms are at stake.        Proper consideration of the law, the

facts, and most critically, the deferential abuse of discretion standard, requires a

different result than the one reached by the majority here. Accordingly, except
